items.title: Was This How Henry VIII Ate Cucumbers? | Historic Cookery at Kew Palace
items.description:
It's likely Henry VIII ate cucumbers, as did his wives Katherine of Aragon and Jane Seymour, but they didn't eat them cold in salads. The Tudors believed cold and wet foods were bad for you, so they boiled cucumbers with meat!

items.title: The Dessert Topping That Was Invented To Be A Medicine
items.description:
Chocolate is one of the world's favorite treats, but once upon a time it was actually considered a medication. Yes, for centuries, doctors believed chocolate could cure everything from fatigue to digestive problems, and it was often mixed into bizarre medicinal recipes. So how did this ancient "health food" transform into the sweet dessert topping we know today?

items.title: Philosophy books that changed how I see the world
items.description:
Books, unlike any other form of media, have a way of shifting our perspectives. Today, I want to share 5 books with you that had that effect on me: a recent book on privacy, Hannah Arendt's work on the vita activa, Russell on idleness, some Byung-Chul Han, and the fiction of Jorge Louis Borges. 

My interview with Lowry Pressly on the right to privacy: https://jaredhenderson.substack.com/p/the-right-to-oblivion-an-interview

Read books with me over on Substack: https://jaredhenderson.substack.co

The puss named Millie was first owned by Leslie Greenhough’s late wife, who took her in as a 3-month-old kitten. Leslie told SWNS news agency that Millie’s long lifespan is a result of giving her only natural […] The post World’s Oldest Cat Drinks Only Spring Water as She Celebrates 31 Years Old appeared first on Good News Network .
global_silver_linings.reason: At 31 years old, this remarkable cat is a living reminder that small, consistent acts of care — like offering fresh spring water — can nurture a life well beyond all expectations. There's something quietly wonderful about an animal that has shared three decades with the humans who love her.

featured_read.title: Darwin’s Greatest Regret and His Deathbed Reflection on What Makes Life Worth Living
featured_read.snippet: "If I had to live my life again, I would have made a rule to read some poetry and listen to some music at least once every week."
featured_read.blurb: Darwin mapped the architecture of life itself, yet spent his final years mourning the slow death of his own capacity for beauty — a quietly devastating warning about what we trade away when we let wonder go fallow. This one asks whether the most rigorous minds are also the most vulnerable to a particular kind of impoverishment.
